2674.tone: Source is a first-hand description treating Mbukushu as a lexical H/L tone language: sonogram counts of HH/HL/LH/LL words (prefix omitted as low), 'the vowels usually carry the tone', m/n act as depressors creating rising/falling contours (nyàtjí 'buffalo', mwána 'child'), H may sit on the prefix ku- (kúfa 'die'); dictionary entries carry high-tone accents, and lexical tone is defined as the pattern of the word in isolation (not the phrase-final pattern, contra Hannam's Shona dictionary). Secondary (Sommer 2003, Routledge Bantu Languages ch. 28, in the copy consulted) notes that lexical tone 'has sometimes been mentioned' for Mbukushu (dí-na 'louse' vs dì-na 'name') while 'others... opine that tone as such is not distinctive within the Kavango group', and describes stress/accent/length interaction only for Gciriku (Möhlig 1997:220), nothing for Mbukushu.

2679.tone: Source: three word-level pitch levels, low (`), high (¯), superhigh (´), 'both lexically and grammatically'; the superhigh level 'is best described as phonological stress rather than tone (s. Diehl 2007)'; a few high-low (falling) combinations within one mora (bɔ̄̀r 'honey'); tone not used for case; number marking sometimes uses tone changes (pl. sīsò, sg. sīsòč 'bee'); demonstrative clitics are toneless. The entry's transcriptions mark the superhigh on more than one mora in many words (kɔ́náŋ 'one', súsá 'sun', ám-óŋ, k-ús-óŋ, šéššék-ɔ́, báyít), and the superhigh is used grammatically (ām 'he/she eats/ate' with high vs ám-óŋ negated with superhigh), so nothing in the opened source establishes culminativity or a position for the superhigh/stress. Secondary reports of Diehl 2007 (not opened): Pilaszewicz review (SALC 41, pp. 161-162) says Diehl 'tries to explain why certain toneless morphemes in Me'en... trigger pitch-raising retroactively' and concludes the phenomenon 'needs to be recorded in the lexicon, since it is part of the morpheme's lexical properties' (p. 87); JALL 30 (2009) Google Books: 'makes an argument that the ultra-High tone in Me'en is in fact the realization of stress on a high tone. While this resolves the question of the distributional properties of the ultra-high...'. Will 1989 p. 130 (Rosetta Project scan): 'Tone and stress have not yet been sufficiently investigated.'

2681.heavy: No weight condition stated. The minor/major distinction is structural (a presyllable with a reduced or superscript vowel, e.g. Mel kətʊːl ~ kᵊtʊːl 'abdomen', lᵊpiət 'tongue', ᵊraw 'wash'; Khaonh kəndʊl, ᵐpeæt; Table 4, p. 11), so the statement could be re-read as full-vs-reduced-vowel weight, but the source states it positionally (first syllable unstressed, following syllable stressed).
2681.prule: Words are monosyllables or sesquisyllables (minor presyllable + major syllable); the initial minor syllable is unstressed and the following (word-final) major syllable is stressed, i.e. stress on the final/main syllable. Stated of Bahnaric languages generally ('Bahnaric languages, like other Mon-Khmer languages, are sesquisyllabic'), not of Mel or Khaonh forms specifically. The report does NOT classify Mel and Khaonh outright: sec. 1.2 says 'Neither Mel nor Khaonh languages have been classified linguistically, though they are most lexically similar to languages in the South Bahnaric sub-branch of Eastern Mon-Khmer', and Gregerson (2010) is reported as having 'tentatively' found that they 'appear on first inspection to be South Bahnaric'. The authors nonetheless apply the sesquisyllable premise to the Mel and Khaonh wordlists, stripping minor syllables before lexical comparison. FAMILY-LEVEL GENERIC (Bahnaric/Mon-Khmer), NOT LANGUAGE-SPECIFIC; classification itself tentative.

2681.quote: Bahnaric languages, like other Mon-Khmer languages, are sesquisyllabic. Sesquisyllabic languages have a minor syllable and a major syllable. The minor syllable comes first and is unstressed while the following major syllable is stressed. Over time, these minor syllables are subject to innovation and sometimes collapse onto the main syllable, while the major syllable is usually retained and can be reliably reconstructed. 2686.prule: No word stress. Syllables of an utterance are 'evenly stressed'; the source denies any accentual pattern belonging to the word, the phrase or the sentence beyond the succession of syllable tones. Prosody is a four-toneme syllable-tone system (high, low, falling, rising; the inflected tones only on long vowels or vowel clusters), the word's pitch melody being the sum of its syllables' tonemes (Hoijer's type 3, syllable toneme, not a word-accent system).
2686.srule: None: no stress contrast of any degree is described ('a succession of evenly stressed syllables... there are no distinctive accentual patterns characteristic of the word, the phrase, or the sentence'); prominence is syllable tone only, so there is no secondary stress to place.

Pronominal suffixes count in the window (u̯äläd'nä, u̯äläd'kum). Jastrow's pan-Mesopotamian statement of the same rule: the first v̄K or vKK group counted from the word end is stressed, at the latest the third-from-last vowel (Bagdad Muslim ḍúrbat, ḍurbátni).

2689.dq: In most languages stress, a slight raise of the pitch, is not relevant.
2689.dloc: ch. 23, p. 539, section 'Stress'; Masqan placed in Western Gurage (outside PWG) on pp. 535-536.
2689.prule: No stress position is stated for Masqan. The only statement bearing on it is group-level: in most Outer South Ethiopic languages stress, 'a slight raise of the pitch', is 'not relevant' (non-distinctive); only Peripheral Western Gurage (PWG: Inor, Endegen, Gyeto, Ener) has a grammatically meaningful stress system, and the rule that follows (final closed syllable stressed, otherwise penultimate; final -e/-i always stressed; accentual harmony) is explicitly Inor's and does not apply to Masqan, which Hetzron places in Western Gurage outside PWG (p. 535).

2691.dq: [p. 108] the accent rule counts syllables starting at the end of the word proceeding leftward, whereas the strong syllable rule starts at the beginning of words and proceeds rightward
2691.dloc: Costa 2003 p. 108, section 3.2.7 'Accent' (page number as returned by Google Books view, volume qCyE8fR12HsC)
2691.heavy: Long vowels: 'Words with long vowels in their preantepenultimate syllables regularly take accent on the antepenultimate syllable' (p. 114). Conversely, devoiced vowels (short vowels in weak, odd-numbered syllables before a preaspirate) 'cannot receive accent' (p. 113). Consonant codas play no stated role except via preaspirates triggering devoicing.
2691.dflt: penultimate (final in disyllables whose first vowel is short and devoiced before a preaspirate, e.g. ahkí 'field', mahkwá 'bear')
2691.prule: Accent is assigned right-to-left, independently of the left-to-right iambic 'strong syllable rule'. Default: penultimate syllable (all disyllables without a medial preaspirate; 'basic' in most longer words). Quantity condition: if the preantepenultimate syllable has a long vowel, accent falls on the antepenult instead ('accent retraction', p. 114), unless the antepenult is devoiced (p. 117) or the penult precedes a preaspirate (p. 118). Devoiced vowels (short vowels in weak syllables before a preaspirate) can never carry accent (p. 113), so CVhCV disyllables are final-accented (ahkí 'field', mahkwá 'bear') and a devoiced penult passes accent to the antepenult.
2691.srule: Alternating: accent falls on every other syllable counting leftward from the end of the word, so words of five or more syllables carry accent on both the preantepenultimate and the penultimate syllable (hedged 'Apparently'); devoiced vowels cannot be accented. The source does not rank these accents as primary vs secondary.

2692.dq: Segundo, el acento y el tono distintivo caen en la primera sílaba del radical simple (o compuesto), el tono de la segunda sílaba del radical (o formativo temático) es totalmente predecible

2692.prule: Stress, together with the lexically distinctive tone, falls on the first syllable of the simple (or compound) radical, i.e. the root syllable; the second syllable of the radical (the stem formative, or an object suffix) is the weak branch of a syllabic trochee. TAM/person proclitics precede the stressed root syllable outside the foot; monosyllabic roots are rearticulated to CV.ʔV in isolation ([ˈpa˨.ʔa˨] 'irse') to fill the trochee. Position is thus defined by morphology (root-initial), equivalent to phonological-word-initial since the p-word begins at the root.

2692.tone: Tonal language with four tones: 'La lengua mazahua tiene cuatro tonos: alto [á], bajo [à], descendente [â] y ascendente [ǎ]' (2024: 47). The contrastive tone sits on the stressed root syllable; the post-tonic formative has predictable tone (low after H/L/HL, high after LH); CVʔCˀV stems allow only H vs L. Stress is described alongside tone as a positional (root-initial) property and is not tonally conditioned; all Tabla 4 IPA forms carry an initial stress mark.
